lesson.title: Counting the Ways: The Hidden Arithmetic Behind Entropy
lesson.summary: A microstate is one exact, fully detailed arrangement of a system's particles, while a macrostate is the observable condition; counting how many microstates correspond to each macrostate explains, with real arithmetic, why systems evolve toward the most probable arrangement.
lesson.body:
The previous chapter argued informally that more spread out arrangements are simply more numerous, and therefore more probable, than concentrated ones. Microstates give that argument a precise vocabulary. A microstate is one complete, specific description of exactly where every particle is and exactly how the system's energy is distributed among them. A macrostate, by contrast, is the observable, measurable condition of the system, such as "the gas occupies the left half of the container" or "the gas is evenly spread through the whole container," without specifying which particle is where. Many different microstates can produce the same macrostate, and the number of microstates corresponding to a given macrostate is usually written W. Systems evolve toward whichever macrostate has the largest W, not because of any active force pushing them there, but because, with huge numbers of particles, that macrostate is so overwhelmingly more probable that any other outcome essentially never happens.

A concrete, fully countable example makes this precise. Imagine two connected, equal-volume glass bulbs, and imagine placing 4 labeled, distinguishable gas molecules somewhere among the two bulbs, with every molecule independently equally likely to be in either bulb. Each molecule has 2 choices (bulb A or bulb B), so the total number of equally likely microstates is 2 to the power 4, which is 16. Now group those 16 microstates by macrostate, defined by how many molecules are in each bulb. All 4 molecules in bulb A (0 in B): there is only 1 way for this to happen, since every specific molecule has to be the one placed in A, so W = 1. Symmetrically, all 4 in bulb B: W = 1. Exactly 3 molecules in bulb A, 1 in bulb B: you are choosing which single molecule is the odd one out in bulb B, and there are 4 molecules that could be that one, so W = 4 (using the combination formula, this is 4 choose 1, or equivalently 4 choose 3, both equal to 4). Symmetrically, 1 in A and 3 in B also gives W = 4. Exactly 2 molecules in each bulb: you are choosing which 2 of the 4 molecules go in bulb A, which is 4 choose 2, equal to 6, so W = 6.

Check that these add up correctly: 1 (all A) + 4 (3A,1B) + 6 (2A,2B) + 4 (1A,3B) + 1 (all B) = 1 + 4 + 6 + 4 + 1 = 16, matching the total of 16 microstates counted directly. Good, the bookkeeping is consistent. The striking result is that the even 2-2 split has, by a wide margin, the most microstates, 6 out of 16, meaning if you set up this experiment and let the molecules move freely between the bulbs, you would find an even split about 6/16, or 37.5 percent, of the time you check, versus only 1/16, about 6 percent, for all 4 molecules bunched into a single bulb.

With only 4 molecules, an all-in-one-bulb outcome is rare but not impossible; you could plausibly observe it if you checked often enough. But real gas samples contain on the order of Avogadro's number of molecules, about 6 x 10^23, not 4. Scaling this same counting logic up to that many particles, the number of microstates corresponding to an even distribution becomes so colossally larger than the number corresponding to any noticeably uneven distribution that the uneven ones are, for all practical purposes, never observed. This is the honest statistical answer to why a gas fills its container evenly and never spontaneously collects itself into one corner: nothing forbids it, it is simply so overwhelmingly improbable, by the same reasoning as this 4-molecule example scaled up trillions of times over, that you could wait far longer than the age of the universe and still not see it happen. Turning W itself into an actual entropy value, in the familiar J/K units used throughout this course, is exactly what the Boltzmann equation does next.
